0.0.n: Used to agree or pick up the conversation.

0.2.n: This is the film's title, written in katakana.

0.3.n: Marks Zootopia as what has been gaining appeal.

0.4.n: Adds a friendly pause that draws the listener in.

0.6.n: Sets the time frame for the speaker's growing interest.

0.7.n: Refers to the speaker here, rather than another person.

0.8.n: Links 自分 to 中 to describe the speaker's personal feelings.

0.9.n: In 自分の中で, this refers figuratively to the speaker's own mind or preferences.

0.10.n: Marks the personal sphere in which Zootopia is gaining appeal.

0.11.n: Strengthens how much Zootopia has been appealing to the speaker.

0.12.n: Short for 来ていて, from 来る; here it casually describes rising personal enthusiasm and connects to what follows.

1.0.n: This is the name of a character in Zootopia.

1.1.n: Identifies Nick as the character being praised.

1.2.n: Invites the listener's attention before the speaker's opinion.

1.4.n: Expresses the speaker's positive opinion of Nick.

1.5.n: Adds an explanatory, personal tone; it does not stand for a thing here.

2.0.n: The character's name is repeated to emphasize the speaker's enthusiasm.

2.1.n: Keeps the repeated praise conversational and engaging.

2.3.n: Casually replaces すごく to strengthen 良い.

2.4.n: Read いい here; it expresses the same praise as in the previous line.

3.0.n: Introduces another character the speaker wants to mention.

3.1.n: Makes あと the topic, shifting attention to another favorite.

3.3.n: This is the name of the sloth character in Zootopia.

4.0.n: This character's name identifies whose manner the speaker is describing.

4.1.n: Links Flash to his distinctive manner.

4.3.n: Points to Flash's recognizable slow manner, assumed to be familiar to the listener.

4.4.n: Describes Flash's unhurried pace in ゆっくりとした.

4.5.n: Pairs with ゆっくり before した to describe how Flash comes across.

4.6.n: Past form of する; in ゆっくりとした, it describes a quality rather than a completed action.

4.7.n: Refers to the overall impression of Flash's manner.

4.8.n: Marks Flash's slow manner as what triggers the reaction in the next line.

4.9.n: Adds a conversational pause before explaining the speaker's reaction.

5.0.n: Emphasizes how strongly the speaker reacts to Flash's manner.

5.1.n: Literally a pot or pressure point; here it means what particularly tickles the speaker's sense of humor.

5.2.n: Marks the target in ツボに入る, an expression for finding something especially funny.

5.3.n: 入っちゃって contracts 入ってしまって, suggesting an unplanned reaction and leaving the thought conversationally open.

6.0.n: Signals that another character has just come to mind.

6.2.n: Adds one more character to the speaker's list.

6.3.n: This is the name of the cheetah character in Zootopia.

6.4.n: Includes Clawhauser among the characters the speaker likes.

6.5.n: Describes fondness; Japanese leaves out the speaker and the casual ending だ here.

7.0.n: The character being described is understood, so no subject needs to be stated.

8.0.n: Softens the observation, suggesting the speaker cannot quite explain the reaction.

8.1.n: Casual contraction of 見ている; the person being watched is understood from context.

8.2.n: Links watching him to a reaction that naturally follows.

8.3.n: Draws the listener in before describing the craving.

8.5.n: The object of eating; the object-marking particle を is omitted in casual speech.

8.6.n: 食べたい expresses desire; its く-form connects to なる to mean becoming hungry for something.

8.7.n: なる becomes なって before くる, presenting the desire as gradually developing.

0.lit: Yeah, Zootopia, you know, recently, within myself, has been coming on quite strongly, and…
0.tip: 自分の中できてる casually means something is gaining appeal for you personally.

1.tip: Sentence-ending の adds a personal, explanatory tone to the praise.

2.tip: In casual speech, すごい can mean really before an adjective, instead of the standard すごく.

3.tip: あとは introduces another item without needing a complete sentence.

4.lit: Flash's, that slow-paced feeling, you know…
4.tip: ゆっくりとした describes a leisurely quality and modifies 感じ, rather than reporting a past action.

5.lit: Quite a bit, it ended up entering my comedic sweet spot.
5.tip: ツボに入る means something hits your particular sense of humor and makes you laugh.

6.lit: Oh, also Clawhauser too, I like.
6.tip: も marks Clawhauser as another character the speaker likes.

7.tip: Japanese often leaves out he or she when the person being described is already clear.

8.lit: Somehow, when watching him, you know, I start becoming wanting to eat doughnuts.
8.tip: 食べたくなってくる describes a desire to eat gradually arising.
